Name: Tim Dees
Question: Could a guy that was diagnosed with autism and had learning disability in school get accepted into the police force or any opportunity at all in law enforcement?
Answer: Possibly. Autism is a “spectrum” disorder, with Rain Man types at one end and people who are just socially awkward at the other. You would need to find a law enforcement agency that was tolerant of personality quirks. You would also need to develop a thick skin, as cops can be very insensitive to oddities among their peers.

Name: Tim Dees
Question: Is a person guilty of an alleged crime they've been charged with, such as shoplifting, if there was no motive or intent, but just a freak occurrence that can be explained?
Answer: I’m not sure how a shoplifting incident can be a “freak occurrence.” Did a rogue wave wash ashore and direct a carton of cigarettes into your pants? You are free to offer nearly any defense to shoplifting you like, but the state is permitted to cross-examine you. That’s usually where the “freak occurrence” defenses come apart. A judge is going to be more lenient to someone who comes clean and admits their crime than with someone who assumes the court is so dumb the offender can get a fantastic story by them.

Name: Tim Dees
Question: Law Enforcement officers, have arrests become significantly more dramatic (e.g., suspects screaming about handcuffs/placement, their arm hurts, etc.) since bodycams became standard practice, or were they always this way?
Answer: People have often complained, but now they are aware they’re being recorded on video, either by the officer or by a bystander/friend, they will exercise the maximum level of drama in an effort to show how viciously they were abused. They’ll collapse and pretend to be unconscious, scream constantly about how much pain they are experiencing, and scream declarations of their violated rights, or what they think are their violated rights. It’s manufactured angst for the benefit of the video. These folks are often previewed the video before they go to court. They seldom elect to show the video in court, or will actively oppose the showing of the video. This is because the casual observer can see that the arrestee was acting childishly or deceptively, and they don’t want that portrayal to be seen by the judge and/or jury. Video encourages good behavior by the cops, but also depicts the demeanor of the defendant that isn’t otherwise seen in court. More than once, I’ve seen someone review an arrest video and then tell the officer, “You must have the patience of a saint.”

Name: Tim Dees
Question: What are the benefits of being a police officer rather than a firefighter?
Answer: The pay, benefits, and pension tend to be about the same. Firefighters have their own fraternity or brotherhood, but it’s distinct from that of the cops. The biggest difference, I think, is that the cop’s job doesn’t end when he goes off duty. He may go off the clock, but he’s likely still carrying his badge and firearm, and may have handcuffs or other police tools with him. He feels the need to be able to react as a police officer should he find himself in a tense situation. Firefighters don’t carry an off-duty axe or Halligan tool (although I have seen some with huge fire extinguishers in their personal cars), and other than the need to perform first aid in some cases, they have no special obligations (official or self-imposed) when they’re off duty. Carrying the gun is a big deal. Most cops experiment with different ways of carrying their gun off duty, and within a few years, have an entire drawer or two full of holsters they tried and discarded. They feel naked if they leave the house without the gun. Having the gun 24/7 also has a high CDI (Chicks Dig It) factor. I got a lot more girls while I was a cop than I did before I was one. I don’t include my post-cop years in that equation, as I was married then. Although one’s police powers generally extended only to the borders of the state where the officer is commissioned, for many years there was a kind of Code of the West practice that an out-of-state cop would not be hassled for carrying his gun so long as he behaved himself. In 2004, this practice was codified in the law with the Law Enforcement Officers Safety Act, and active duty cops could carry their firearms in every state. The privilege is also extended to retired cops with ten years or more of service, providing they qualify with the firearms once a year. Where I live, the local Fraternal Order of Police chapter puts on a qualification session (actually, it takes a couple of days to get everyone through) for retired folks, even ones like me from other states. Thanks to them, I don’t have to feel naked when I leave the house. I may not be a cop anymore, but the awareness of danger never leaves you.

Name: Tim Dees
Question: If there has just been a robbery (example) and there is a description of the vehicle, appearance and/or clothing of a person and officers encounter someone with that description. Can this person be arrested?
Answer: The similarity in description would be sufficient Reasonable Articulable Suspicion (RAS) to stop and detain the person. If the situation was such that the officer could say why he felt the suspect could be armed, he could pat down the suspect for weapons. This is a “Terry Stop,” named for the decision in Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1 (1968). A Terry stop does not permit the officer to remove the suspect from the location he was stopped without the suspect’s consent. To get probable cause for arrest, the officer would do a field interview of the suspect, including taking a photo. The photo would then be included in a “six pack” of photos to show the victim to see if he recognized anyone in the array. If so, the police could obtain an arrest warrant for the suspect. In the alternative, the officer could have another officer pick up the victim and drive by the location where the suspect was stopped to make an identification or say, “No, that’s not the guy.” These identifications are more iffy, as the suggestion that the suspect has been stopped by the police and the lack of other possible suspects is more suggestive of guilt.
